source: Winkler, Smith, Fryback (2002) The role of informative priors in zero-numerator problems: being conservative versus being candid
finding: With zero events seen, the usual 'noninformative' beta priors disagree widely, so they are not really uninformative. An informative prior from a related known rate gives a tight, sensible answer.
numbers: Contrast-agent example, 0 reactions in n=167: under Beta(a,a) priors with 0<a<=1 the posterior 0.95 fractile runs from near 0 up to 0.018 (a=1). For smaller n it can reach 0.133 (n=20) and 0.238 (n=10). With prior mean 0.0015 (old agent) and strength 1 to 5,000 the 0.95 fractile never exceeds 0.004, against 1.8% from the Rule of Three. Elicited Beta(0.042,27.96) prior gives posterior mean 0.022%.
quote: Observing no occurrences of the reaction effectively wipes out the upper end of the U-shaped distribution
limits: Worked example, no replication study; one medical domain. Priors elicited by the authors.
agent_relevance: For a class with no history, a default of Beta(1,1) or Jeffreys is arbitrary and small-n answers swing with it. Prefer a pooled or related-class prior with an explicit strength, and record which default was used.

source: Winkler, Smith, Fryback (2002), Casey example (same paper, second finding)
finding: Being 'conservative' with a prior or bound on an input can backfire downstream. A pessimistic false-positive rate made the diagnosis look less likely, not more.
numbers: Newborn screen: informative Beta(1,999) prior gives posterior Beta(1,13999), mean 1/14,000=0.0000714, diagnostic probability 0.053. Using the Rule-of-Three upper bound gives 0.018 (about 3 times lower). Using the MLE of zero gives probability 1.
limits: Single example. Shows direction of error, not its general size. Same paper as d01, counted as one source.
agent_relevance: If the agent uses a class pass-rate as a gate input, do not shade it for safety. Shading can move the final decision the wrong way. Pass the full (k,n) and compute the gate from the posterior mean.

source: Gelman, Simpson, Betancourt (2017) The prior can generally only be understood in the context of the likelihood
finding: A prior cannot be judged alone. Defaults (uniform, Jeffreys, reference, max-entropy) are all tied to a reference likelihood. Judge a prior by what it implies for predictions (the prior predictive).
numbers: No new experiment counts. Argues a uniform or very broad prior is not a safe default when the true effect is small, because the estimate has error of order n^-1/2 and noise swamps signal.
quote: It's not so much that the uniform prior is inherently bad, but rather that its interaction with the likelihood and the data facilitates poor performance.
limits: Position and methods paper. Few new data. Written for modelling practice, not for LLM agents.
agent_relevance: Supports checking the prior through predictions: a class prior should be tested by what pass rates it would predict, which is the same idea as our prior-predictive doubt check.

source: Nott, Drovandi, Mengersen, Evans (2020) Checking for prior-data conflict using prior-to-posterior divergences
finding: Gives an exact prior-data conflict check for the binomial model: the prior predictive is beta-binomial, and the p-value is the chance of a result at most as surprising as the one seen. Reviews the Evans-Moshonov (2006) check that uses the same predictive.
numbers: Binomial Example 3.2: y~Bin(n,theta), theta~Beta(a,b), prior predictive p(y)=C(n,y)B(a+y,b+n-y)/B(a,b). Check p-value = P(R(Y)>=R(y_obs)) with Y drawn from the prior predictive. The two checks are not equivalent but agree when y and n-y are both large.
quote: these p-values are not measures of evidence, and it may be better to think of the tail probability (3) as a calibration
limits: Authors stress the p-value is a calibration of surprise, not evidence. Checks are not invariant to the choice of statistic in continuous cases. The paper gives no false-alarm table for small n; see d08 for our own computation.
agent_relevance: This is a usable doubt trigger for class records: if the case result lies in the far tail of the beta-binomial built from the class record, raise a doubt step instead of trusting the prior.

source: Own simulation: Brier score of default priors for small classes (n<10)
finding: Synthetic test of gaps 1 and 2. Classes have true pass rates drawn from a Beta with pooled mean 0.6; each class has 0-9 past outcomes; score is expected Brier on the next outcome. Shrinking toward a prior beats raw k/n, and a wrong recalled prior (assumed 0.8) is worse than a flat 0.5.
numbers: Pool strength S=6, M=50 classes, 2000 reps: raw k/n (0.5 if n=0) 0.2678; uniform Beta(1,1) 0.2339; Jeffreys 0.2406; constant 0.5 0.250; recalled prior 0.8 0.2794; empirical Bayes 0.2297. S=2 (M=50): raw 0.2146, uniform 0.1949, EB 0.1953. S=20 (M=50): raw 0.2954, uniform 0.2537, EB 0.2397. Known-prior Bayes with the true Beta: 0.1922 (S=2), 0.2271 (S=6), 0.2380 (S=20).
limits: SYNTHETIC. Assumes pass rates are exchangeable draws from one Beta and outcomes are independent. Real run logs were not tested, so gap 1 stays open for our actual agent. The recalled prior of 0.8 is an assumed bias, not a measured LLM value. Equal tokens not tested.
agent_relevance: Even crude shrinkage of the class record (add 1 success and 1 failure) cut Brier by about 13 percent against raw k/n at n<10. A recall that is 0.2 off costs more than using no class information. Do the shrinkage in code, not in the model.

source: Own simulation: how many classes are needed to set prior strength by empirical Bayes
finding: Method-of-moments beta-binomial strength estimated across classes is very noisy for few classes. A fixed Beta(1,1) beats it when classes are few and true strength is low or moderate.
numbers: Same set-up as d05, S=6: Brier EB vs uniform: M=5 0.2397 vs 0.2342; M=10 0.2351 vs 0.2340; M=20 0.2324 vs 0.2345; M=50 0.2297 vs 0.2339; M=200 0.2285 vs 0.2343. Median estimated strength: 200 (cap) at M=5, 19.9 at M=10, 13.3 at M=20, 9.9 at M=200 (true 6). S=2: EB did not beat uniform until M=200 (0.1937 vs 0.1945). S=20: EB ahead already at M=5 (0.2498 vs 0.2536).
limits: SYNTHETIC; one estimator (method of moments), strength capped at 200, history length uniform 0-9. Better estimators (marginal likelihood, SURE as in d09) may need fewer classes. Rule of thumb only.
agent_relevance: Use a fixed default (Beta(1,1)) until about 20 classes have records, then switch to estimated strength. Cap strength so a few lucky classes do not make the prior stiff.

finding: For a class with no history, Beta(1,1), Jeffreys and Haldane (taken as 0.5 when n=0) all give the same point prediction 0.5. Only a pooled prior moves it. The pooled mean beats 0.5 whenever the pool is not at 0.5.
numbers: Pool mean 0.6. Brier at constant 0.5: 0.250. Brier at pooled mean 0.6: 0.2399 (S=2), 0.2401 (S=6), 0.2399 (S=20). Defaults differ only once n is 1 to 3 and k=0 or k=n, where Haldane would give 0 or 1.
limits: SYNTHETIC. Haldane is improper and gives 0 or 1 after one observation, so it is unusable as a gate input. Result depends on the pool being stable.
agent_relevance: For zero history use the pooled empirical rate, not a flat default. Keep Beta(1,1) only before any pool exists. Never use Haldane for a gate.

source: Own simulation: false-alarm rate and power of the beta-binomial prior-predictive check
finding: The exact beta-binomial check has false-alarm rate at or below alpha, because the outcome is discrete. Its power to catch a true rate of 0.2 against a prior mean of 0.6 is modest at small n.
limits: SYNTHETIC. The 0.051 is within Monte Carlo noise of 0.05 (standard error about 0.0015) plus discreteness. Assumes the prior is correctly specified apart from the conflict under test.
agent_relevance: A doubt trigger at p<0.05 on the case-level (k,n) fires falsely in at most about 5 percent of cases and catches a large shift only about a third of the time when n is 5 to 10. Use it as a cheap flag, not as proof of agreement.

source: Chen and Lei (2025) Compound estimation for binomials
finding: Many binomial rates estimated together: shrinking toward a pooled mean with a data-chosen amount (SURE-tuned) gave the lowest holdout error on all three real datasets, even with very small samples per unit.
numbers: Holdout MSE, binomial-shrinkage estimator vs best Gaussian-EB competitor: innovation rates 2.8666e-5 vs 2.8940e-5; education 0.0246 vs 0.0249; employment discrimination (n=3 per group in training) 0.1204 vs 0.1257 (CLOSE not applicable there).
limits: Table text extracted from the PDF is garbled, so the column mapping is a reading of the layout. Gains are about 1 percent in two datasets. Theory is asymptotic in the number of units. Authors note the binomial prior is not identified.
agent_relevance: Supports estimating shrinkage strength from data across classes rather than fixing it, and shows it is workable with only 3 trials per unit. Gain over simple grand-mean shrinkage may be small.

source: Samanta et al. (2026) BayesBench: LLM belief trajectories under multi-turn evidence accumulation
finding: Seven instruction-tuned models (Llama 3 at 3B, 8B, 70B; Qwen 2.5 at 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B) track a Beta(1,1) coin posterior only roughly over 100 flips. Small models under-update, large models over-update toward 0 or 1. Gains in inferring the latent do not carry over to downstream prediction.
numbers: Coin bias 0.25, 0.5, 0.75; T=100 flips; dialogue temperature 0.7, beliefs read from log-probabilities. Single-turn vs multi-turn delivery changes trajectories, with the gap largest for small models. Also a cold-start recommender task (T=50 ratings, 4 profiles) and a medical triage task. Exact MAE values are in appendix tables that were not read.
limits: No reasoning models. Trends read from figures and text, not from tables. The coin task uses a flat prior, so it does not test prior recall.
agent_relevance: Even the larger models drift off the Bayes posterior in prose. Another reason to compute the posterior in code and show the model the result.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak, An (2026) CogBias (re-opened for Tables 2 and 3)
finding: On three non-reasoning models, prompt-level debiasing made Judgment-family answers (base-rate, anchoring, sunk cost, status quo) slightly worse, while it fixed position bias.
numbers: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen2.5-72B at T=0. Judgment bias shift: -4.3, -7.7, -2.7 pp. Debiasing effect: Judgment accuracy -4.4 percent (backfires), Info Processing -1.1, Social +5.9, Response position independence +40.5.
limits: Does not isolate base-rate items. Not a reasoning-model test. The natural-frequency benefit for LLMs (Dasgupta 2022) is only cited, not measured, so gap 3 is still second-hand.
agent_relevance: A prompt line saying 'consider the base rate' cannot be assumed to help. Give the base rate as a computed number in a labelled field and test it on our own tasks.

source: Pournemat et al. (2025) Reasoning under uncertainty: probabilistic reasoning capabilities of LLMs
finding: Given samples from a discrete distribution in the prompt, models find the mode well when large, but accuracy falls as the label set or sample list grows, and changes with label wording even when counts are fixed.
numbers: Joint-mode accuracy at |L|=12/27/36/54: Llama3.1-8B 0.59/0.57/0.35/0.21; Qwen2.5-7B 0.93/0.83/0.81/0.65; DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B 0.95/0.93/0.91/0.86; Llama3.3-70B 1.00/1.00/1.00/0.97; GPT-4.1-mini 1.00/1.00/0.99/0.96. Authors say counting becomes a challenge as samples grow and recommend a code interpreter or an in-context example.
limits: About raw sample lists, not (k,n) summaries, so only indirect evidence for gap 3. Six models, none a frontier reasoning model. The reasoning-distilled 7B beat the plain 7B and 8B models.
agent_relevance: Show the model a pre-computed (k,n) or effective sample size, never a raw list to count. Label and notation changes alone can shift answers, so keep the display format fixed.

source: Chlon et al. (2026, v3) LLMs are Bayesian in expectation, not in realization
finding: Models change next-token probabilities when the same examples are listed in a different order, which an exact Bayesian posterior would not do. The paper prices this in log loss instead of calling it a refutation.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B/14B, support 256: one-step excess code length 0.020/0.011 bits for Bernoulli prediction and 0.039/0.022 bits for four-way categorical prediction.
limits: Only two Qwen sizes. Mostly theory on order sensitivity, not on prior use.
agent_relevance: Order of items in a class-record list affects the model slightly. Put the summary statistic first and fix the order of entries.

source: Atwell et al. (2026, v6) BASIL: Bayesian assessment of sycophancy in LLMs (re-opened)
finding: Confirms that calibrating the model's stated prior alone raises Bayesian error, while calibrating the prior and rescaling the posterior lowers it.
numbers: Hypothesis III: priors-only calibration increases Bayesian error; calibrating both prior and posterior decreases it. Exact error values are in Figure 3, which was not read.
limits: Same paper as earlier lines c12 and c13; counted as one source. Sycophancy tasks, not class records.
agent_relevance: If we swap a recalled prior for a stored one, the downstream update step should be recomputed as well, not patched.

source: Scholten, Rebholz, Huetter (2024) Metacognitive myopia in large language models
finding: Theory paper. Argues LLMs neglect base rates in conditional computation because training data do not show true base rates, so they keep pre-trained base rates that may not match the real frequency.
numbers: No experiments on base rates. Lists base-rate neglect as one of five symptoms.
quote: unconditional sampling carries the risk of conserving LLMs pre-trained base rates that could be incongruent with the true frequencies
limits: Conceptual framework only. Evidence is borrowed from other work.
agent_relevance: Supports not trusting the model's unconditional prior for a specific class. The support is theoretical.

source: Search note: no study found that tests 2025-2026 reasoning models on base-rate use
finding: Several web searches found nothing on reasoning models and base rates. The newest items (CogBias April 2026, BayesBench June 2026, Pournemat 2025) use GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3 or 3.3, Qwen 2.5 or a 7B R1 distill.
numbers: All 8 allowed WebSearch calls used. arXiv, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex APIs returned 429 or zero-credit on 3 November 2026, so forward-citation lookups failed.
limits: Absence of evidence under rate limits, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. Test reasoning models on our own base-rate probes before relying on any claim.
